summary: Adversarially review the publishable HMTc infant-formula standard across 5 independent lenses

confirmed.location: Draft §6 "The ratchet," lines 129-131: "Roughly four in five brands in the regulated market meet this initial standard; that fraction is deliberate — high enough that good performers can certify now, and designed to fall as the standard tightens."
confirmed.problem: The recommended action (drop the specific numeric pass-rate from this published, consumer-facing standard) is worth applying, but two of the finding's premises are wrong and it is over-severe. (1) The Part 19 citation is misapplied: this document is HMTc program material, not a wiki page (header "HMTc Certification Standard"; footer "published separately from the Heavy Metal Index literature reference"), so it is on the correct side of the firewall. The ~80% figure is method-level DESIGN INTENT, not the per-cell percentile arithmetic Part 19 walls off — docs/standards-methodology.md line 3 says method "is publishable... per-cell arithmetic and the excluded-jurisdiction list may not," and hmtc-governing-principles.md "lead[s] with intent (the row-level pass rate the program is calibrated to)." It is not a firewall breach. (2) It is not a "hidden admission": the draft already openly states the mark "is a testing-and-verification claim, not a safety claim" and never claims exceptional quality, so a pass-rate does not contradict any claim it makes. The genuine, repo-grounded defect is different: standards-methodology.md defines the ~80% as a "monitored average, not a per-category hard cap" that rolls up program-wide (no-dirty-sibling categories admit ~90%), yet §6 states it as a precise measured fact about THIS category ("this initial standard") and about "the regulated market" (the methodology's admission is relative to the certification-relevant pool, not the whole regulated market). That false precision, plus handing a consumer-facing published standard a quotable pass-rate line, justifies removal — as major, not critical (no safety error, no build-blocking breach).
confirmed.fix: In §6, delete the sentence "Roughly four in five brands in the regulated market meet this initial standard; that fraction is deliberate" and describe only the mechanism, which the draft already carries: §3 ("a limit that a large majority of well-controlled brands can meet") and the surviving §6 clause ("high enough that good performers can certify now, and designed to fall as the standard tightens"). Keep the specific admission figure in the records/on-request tier the draft already establishes in §3 ("computational detail... available to auditors and regulators on request"). Do NOT cite Part 19 as the reason in the commit — the accurate rationale is (a) precision: a program-wide monitored design average must not be stated as a measured per-category / whole-regulated-market fact, and (b) do not print a quotable pass-rate in the published consumer-facing standard.

confirmed.location: §4 table ("How HMTc compares to law", lines 91-97) vs §2 table soy column (soy Ni 400, soy Al 4600, lines 42/44) and §3 regulatory-ceiling rule (lines 76-78)
confirmed.problem: Real, publication-blocking facial contradiction — but the finding mischaracterizes it. §3 promises "No HMTc limit exceeds the lowest maximum level in force ... in any comparable jurisdiction"; §4 lists "Lowest applicable legal ML" as Ni 250 and Al 3500 with a NON-SOY-ONLY column and no soy rows; yet §2 certifies soy at Ni 400 and Al 4600 and labels both "regulatory ceiling." As printed, the soy limits appear to sit above the document's own stated ceilings — precisely the self-impeachment a plaintiff's expert or QA reviewer would seize on. The finding's premise that a limit is actually set ABOVE the law is FALSE: repo regulatory data confirms soy-specific higher MLs exist — EU 2024/1987 sets Ni 400 for soy-protein-isolate powder (vs 250 non-soy), and AU/NZ Sch 19 sets Al 1000 as-consumed for soy (vs 500 non-soy), which at the program's 1:7 factor is 7000 powder. Soy Ni 400 = its soy ceiling (400); soy Al 4600 is BELOW its soy ceiling (7000). The standard is legally defensible; the defect is that §4 omits the soy MLs, and §2 mislabels soy Al as "regulatory ceiling" when 4600 is below the 7000 soy ceiling (it is a testing baseline). The finding's proposed fix (b) — capping soy Ni at 250 and soy Al at 3500 — would introduce a genuine error by discarding the valid soy MLs.
confirmed.fix: Apply the finding's option (a), not (b). In §4, add soy rows with the real soy MLs and citations: Nickel soy — HMTc 400, legal ML 400, EU 2024/1987 (soy-protein-isolate powder row); Aluminium soy — HMTc 4600, legal ML 7000 (AU/NZ Sch 19 soy row, 1000 as-consumed x7 converted). Reword §3 from "lowest maximum level in force for the product in any comparable jurisdiction" to "lowest applicable ML for the product subcategory." In §2, change the soy Aluminium basis label from "regulatory ceiling" to "testing baseline," since 4600 is below the 7000 soy ceiling (the soy Nickel "regulatory ceiling" label is correct, since 400 = the soy ML). Do not cap the soy limits at the non-soy ceilings.

confirmed.location: §3 "a percentile of the metal's measured occurrence" and "Subcategory calibration" ("a large majority can meet" / "admits only its cleaner producers"); §3 & §8 "per-product computational detail... available to auditors and regulators on request"
confirmed.problem: The draft withholds the central methodological parameter. §3 says only "a percentile" and calibrates subcategories qualitatively; §3/§8 route the derivation to "on request." The governing method — clean subcategory = P97, dirty = P45 of the subcategory's pooled distribution, final = min(pooled percentile, lowest applicable ML), pool restricted to the certification-relevant market — is explicitly publishable on the HMTc property per the firewall (docs/standards-methodology.md: "method may be published on the HMTc property; per-cell arithmetic and the excluded-jurisdiction list may not"; hmtc-governing-principles.md Principle 4). The firewall bars only per-cell arithmetic and the excluded-jurisdiction list, not the method itself, and the governing principles are built around an adversarial reader who already knows it is P97 ("attacking 'why P97' must instead attack 'why 90%'"), which presupposes disclosure. By hiding the method this document, whose entire purpose is legal defensibility, forgoes its strongest Daubert shield and leaves the six testing-baseline limits underivable from published text. Correction to the reviewer: the finding is overstated. The two regulatory-ceiling rows (Ni 250, Al 3500) ARE reproducible from the published text — §4 shows them equal to the cited MLs — so it is not "none of the eight." And a certification standard is not itself expert testimony: compliance is fully testable (COA vs. limit) and "derivation on request" is a recognized, defensible posture (Prop 65 MADLs, most eco-labels). This is a real, cheap, should-fix strengthening, not a fatal "black box" or a publication blocker — hence major, not critical.
confirmed.fix: State the method in-text, which the firewall permits on this HMTc document: clean subcategory limit = P97 and dirty = P45 of that subcategory's pooled occurrence distribution; final limit = min(pooled percentile, lowest applicable ML) in the row's native basis; pool admission restricted to markets enforcing binding formula MLs with comparable surveillance (the market-scope criterion). Tie it to §6 by noting P97/P45 is the per-analyte uplift calibrated to deliver the ~90% clean / ~40% dirty row-pass intent that rolls up to the "four in five" figure. Keep the per-product arithmetic, per-cell pool, and excluded-jurisdiction list in the staff workbench per the firewall. Do NOT adopt the reviewer's promise that "an outside statistician can reproduce each §2 value" — several testing-baseline limits are provisional/thin-data (§7, e.g. tin and the soy subcategory with largely non-detect surveys) and would not reproduce as a clean P97; scope the published claim to "the method and pool-admission criterion are stated here; per-cell computation is retained and available to auditors and regulators," so the standard is not exposed to an expert who reproduces P97 from the source list and gets a different number.

confirmed.location: publishable-draft.md §2 (lead row, 12 vs 2.5, lines 37 and 49-52) against §1/§7 (lines 15-16, 138); verified against data/evidence/hmtc_aggregate_distributions.csv rows infant-formula-powder-non-soy and infant-formula-powder-soy-based, and data/workbench/standards/2026-08-03-methodology-evolution-proposal.md
confirmed.problem: The draft should not ship as written, and the underlying data make the exposure worse than the finding states. The document concedes lead has "no established safe intake" / "protective intake is zero," then certifies cow-milk formula (the product the large majority of formula-fed infants consume) at Pb 12 while holding soy at 2.5 — a ~5x internal disparity on a no-threshold neurotoxin in a litigation-defensibility standard. Repo ground truth: non-soy 12 is the clean-subcategory P97; soy 2.5 is the DIRTY-subcategory P45. The two subcategories' lead occurrence is nearly identical (soy pool p95=11.9, p97=12.8 vs non-soy p97≈12), so the 5x gap is produced almost entirely by branch assignment (clean-P97 vs dirty-P45), not by any difference in contamination. Two of the finding's premises are mechanically wrong and must not be carried to Karen as stated: (1) soy 2.5 is NOT proof "2.5 is achievable" — it is a P45, meaning ~55% of soy products already exceed it; (2) the gap is NOT biology. The draft's own §2 justification ("those metals have no inherent reason to be elevated in soy") is flatly contradicted by the certifier's pool (soy lead ≈ cow-milk lead) and is itself a Part 2 violation — a threshold rationale dressed as more evidence-based than the data support. A plaintiff's expert gets a stronger slide than the finding imagined: identical measured lead, 5x-different limits by bucket, no safe dose, looser limit on the more-consumed product, and a published rationale the certifier's own data disprove.
confirmed.fix: Surface to Karen as a substantive standard-setting/framing decision; do not auto-edit the value. Reject the finding's proposed remedy of "add a sourced biology explanation so the gap reads as biology" — the repo shows no biological difference, so writing one would be fabrication and would deepen the Part 2 over-rationalization. Correct actions: (1) Strike the §2 sentence attributing the lead/mercury/tin soy limits to "no inherent reason to be elevated in soy" — the pool shows soy Pb top-tail ≈ non-soy Pb top-tail. (2) Disclose honestly that soy is the higher-contamination (dirty) subcategory held to a P45 target and non-soy is the clean subcategory held to P97, so the reader is not left believing soy is cleaner. (3) Decide whether a 5x lead disparity driven by branch assignment on near-identical occurrence is defensible for a no-safe-dose neurotoxin on the majority-consumed product, or whether the cow-milk lead treatment should be reconsidered (e.g., toward the demonstrated target-market floor — FDA 2026 reports non-soy Pb p95 ≈ 0.5 ppb prepared-for-feeding) rather than the P97 market ceiling. Ship none of the lead disparity with its current unsupported justification.

confirmed.location: §5 Chromium, final sentence (draft line 120): "This is a process-control tripwire; the chromium itself (trivalent, poorly absorbed) is not a health concern at these levels."
confirmed.problem: The document twice states the mark makes no safety claim — §1 (line 14): "The mark is a testing-and-verification claim, not a safety claim... this standard does not assert that any limit represents a safe level," reinforced by §7 (line 137): "It does not certify safety." §5 then affirmatively characterizes a measured contaminant concentration as "not a health concern at these levels." That is an internal contradiction: the certifier disclaims safety representations, then vouches for the safety of a contaminant level. It is exactly the certifier-vouches-for-safety representation the project's governance is designed to withhold (CLAUDE.md Part 2, and the litigation-defensibility frame in Part 12), and it appears in a published certification standard, making it the representation a plaintiff's expert would quote. The clause is not load-bearing: §5's operational meaning (no hexavalent-Cr health limit; total Cr as a manufacturing screen with a 100 µg/kg equipment-review tripwire) survives intact without it.
confirmed.fix: Delete the health-reassurance clause. End the sentence at the operational fact, e.g.: "This is a process-control tripwire, not a health limit." Retain only that total Cr >=100 µg/kg triggers an equipment-contact review before certification. Do not characterize any measured contaminant level as "not a health concern" (or otherwise safe) anywhere in the document; this §5 clause is the only such affirmative vouch, so no other edits are required.

confirmed.location: §1 lines 17–19 ("cleaner part of the regulated market," "toward cleaner product"); §2 line 47 ("cleaner part of the regulated market"); §3 line 60 ("Whichever is more protective governs") and lines 70–72 ("cleaner subcategory," "cleaner producers"). Correction to the finding's own location string: "more protective" appears in §3, not §4; §4 (lines 100–101) contains only the "25–45% below the legal ceiling" numeric comparison, which carries no health adjective.
confirmed.problem: The document twice states in the plainest terms that the mark is "not a safety claim" and "does not assert that any limit represents a safe level," then describes its own limits with health-connoting vocabulary that invites the reasonable-consumer inference certified = safer. "More protective" is the load-bearing defect: a limit called "more protective" is a direct health representation about the limit, and it contradicts the disclaimer in the same document. It is also gratuitous — the repo's canonical methodology (CLAUDE.md Part 19; docs/governance/hmtc-governing-principles.md:144) defines this exact rule value-neutrally as min(pooled percentile, lowest regulatory ceiling), "the cap binds"/"the percentile binds," with no "protective" language. "Cleaner"/"cleaner product" in the public-facing prose is a secondary but real purity signal to a parent (clean/dirty is legitimate internal P97/P45 jargon, but this is a published standard, not the staff workbench). This internal disclaim-then-connote tension is precisely the attack line the project's defensibility posture exists to foreclose, so it is material, not cosmetic, for a document about to be published.
confirmed.fix: Replace §3 "Whichever is more protective governs" with "The lower of the two governs" — this removes the health inference and realigns the draft to its own canonical min() framing. Neutralize "cleaner" in the public-facing prose: §1/§2 "cleaner part of the regulated market" → "lower-occurrence portion of the market"; §1 "toward cleaner product" → "toward lower-occurrence product"; §3 "cleaner subcategory"/"cleaner producers" → "lower-baseline subcategory"/"lower-baseline producers" (pairing with the draft's existing "higher-baseline subcategory"). Do NOT strip the §4 "25–45% below the legal ceiling" statement — it is a true, adjective-free, load-bearing fact; keep it as written and simply do not add any "protective" gloss to it. Leave §7's "the protective intake is zero" untouched (there "protective" correctly describes a toxicological intake, not the certification limit).

confirmed.location: §7 caveat ("largely non-detects") and the Tin (Sn) row of the §2 limits table (49 non-soy / 4.7 soy)
confirmed.problem: Verified against data/evidence/hmtc_aggregate_distributions.csv and wiki/sources/fsa2016-infant-food-formula-metals-survey.md. Both certified tin limits rest on a single source (FSA 2016) whose tin measurements are largely non-detect: dry non-soy and dry soy formula both reported as Sn 0-23 ug/kg (lower-to-upper bound, lower bound 0), and the source page itself flags its lower/upper-bound non-detect handling. The pooling engine reconstructed the distribution via lognormal_lod_censored_midpoint with weak:true on every contribution and zero sample-level data. From that censored pool it read non-soy P97 = 48.99 (draft 49) and soy P45 = 4.69 (draft 4.7). Two facts make this worse than the finding states: (1) the non-soy P97 (49) extrapolates ABOVE the survey's own observed maximum (23), a degenerate-upper-tail artifact the repo's contamination-profile integrity audit exists to catch, with a 26-67 CI; (2) tin has no regulatory cap backstop (draft §4 confirms; CSV shows no regulatory reference loaded), so unlike Pb/Cd/Ni/Al there is nothing but the artifact-prone occurrence percentile setting the limit. The draft presents these as firm "testing baseline" limits in §2, and the §7 "provisional" disclosure does not cure a number that is a statistical artifact. In a standard whose stated audience includes class-action legal review, this is a genuine defensibility liability, not a stylistic nit.
confirmed.fix: For tin, do not publish an occurrence-percentile limit off the censored single-source pool. Preferred: hold tin as "monitored, not limited" until real detections accumulate, or set an explicit LOQ-based floor and label that basis. If the numbers are kept, they must not appear as firm "testing baseline" values in §2: mark them provisional at the point of the number, disclose the detection frequency and the censoring-handling method (lognormal LOD-censored midpoint, single FSA 2016 survey), and note that the non-soy P97 (49) exceeds the survey's observed maximum (23). Apply the same treatment to the soy P45 tin cell (n=10, censored). This does not require reworking the whole document — it scopes to the tin row plus a one-line methods note.

confirmed.location: §5 Chromium — "The carcinogenic species, hexavalent chromium, is not established as present in this product" / "does not detect it in infant formula above the method's quantification limit"
confirmed.problem: Hexavalent chromium is the one no-threshold carcinogen in the standard, and HMTc sets NO limit on it, justifying that with absence-of-evidence phrasing ("not established as present"; "does not detect it above the method's quantification limit"). For a no-threshold carcinogen in a litigation-facing certification standard — the single highest-scrutiny line in the document — "not detected above the LOQ" is not "not present," and a plaintiff's expert can attack that the certifier declined to set any limit on the carcinogen and leaned on the sensitivity of its own assay. The soft phrasing invites exactly that attack. Note the corpus actually supports a STRONGER, measured claim than the draft's hedge, so the current wording also undersells the evidence: Saraiva 2021 (SS-ID-HPLC-ICP-MS, the gold-standard method that detects and corrects Cr(III)->Cr(VI) interconversion artifacts) found Cr(VI) < LOQ 0.049 µg/kg in n=10 infant-formula milk samples and Cr present exclusively as Cr(III); Song 2024 found Cr(VI) < LOD 0.1 µg/kg in milk powder; EFSA 2014 / Milacic & Scancar 2020 attribute historical detections to interconversion artifacts. The finding's framing slightly under-credits this affirmative evidence, but its core point stands: the justification is phrased as a soft denial rather than a precise measured result, and the numeric LOQ that would make it defensible is available in the corpus and omitted from the draft.
confirmed.fix: Replace "not established as present" with a numeric, measured statement drawn from the corpus: Cr(VI) is measured below the limit of quantification of species-specific isotope-dilution HPLC-ICP-MS (approximately 0.05 µg/kg; Saraiva 2021, n=10 infant-formula milk; corroborated at < 0.1 µg/kg by Song 2024), the method that also demonstrates chromium is present exclusively as trivalent chromium and corrects for the species-interconversion artifacts responsible for historical Cr(VI) detections. State the LOQ number explicitly, describe certified lots as screened against that LOQ, and add a commitment to periodic speciated Cr-VI verification (e.g., tie a Cr-VI speciation confirmation to the existing 100 µg/kg total-chromium tripwire). This converts a soft denial into a defensible measured statement and surfaces evidence that is actually stronger than the current wording implies.

confirmed.location: publishable-draft.md §2 "The certification limits" table, Aluminium (Al) row, soy-based cell (line 44: value 4600, basis "regulatory ceiling"); and §4 "How HMTc compares to law" table (lines 91–97), which has no soy column.
confirmed.problem: The soy-based aluminium limit is published as 4600 µg/kg labeled "regulatory ceiling," but neither part is correct. The AU/NZ Sch 19 soy-formula Al ML is 1000 µg/kg on the portion-ordinarily-consumed (as-consumed) basis; converted to the row's native powder basis at 1:7 it is 1000 × 7 = 7000 µg/kg, not 4600. The program's own crosswalk (product_regulatory_crosswalk.csv line 258) records this exactly: soy Al ceiling = 7000 ppb powder-equivalent, with the pooled literature P97 (6852) binding just below it. So 4600 matches neither the converted ceiling (7000) nor the binding value the methodology yields (min(6852, 7000) = 6852), and it traces to no figure in the evidence register — its only occurrence in the repo is an illustrative line in the ratified methodology proposal that itself disagrees with the crosswalk. The basis label is also wrong on its own terms: per the crosswalk the literature value binds, so the basis is "testing baseline," not "regulatory ceiling" (the ceiling, 7000, does not bind). The adjacent non-soy Al cell (3500 = 500 × 7, ceiling correctly binds since P97 6041 > 3500) is right, which makes the soy cell internally inconsistent with the document's own methodology. Because this is the binding certification table of a flagship standard about to be published, an underivable number carrying a false statement about the law is a direct hit on the traceability/defensibility the standard depends on.
confirmed.fix: Replace 4600 in the soy-based Aluminium cell. Per crosswalk line 258 the literature binds, so the methodologically correct entry is 6852 µg/kg with basis "testing baseline" (matching how the other occurrence-derived soy cells are labeled). If HMTc instead intends the ceiling to govern, use 7000 µg/kg (1000 portion-basis × 7) and keep "regulatory ceiling" — but that contradicts the crosswalk's "literature binds" finding, so 6852 / testing baseline is preferred. Also revise the §2 narrative sentence that attributes the higher soy Al to the law setting a higher ceiling, since for aluminium the occurrence value (not the ceiling) is what binds. Finally, add a soy column to the §4 compare-to-law table so soy Al is shown against its 7000 (converted) AU/NZ Sch 19 ceiling, consistent with how non-soy Al is displayed.

confirmed.location: §4 "How HMTc compares to law", draft line 99: "For total mercury and tin, no jurisdiction sets a formula maximum level; the HMTc limit is set from measured occurrence."
confirmed.problem: The blanket claim is factually overstated for tin. EU Regulation 2023/915 Annex I §3.5.3 does set a tin maximum level of 50,000 µg/kg (50 mg/kg) for infant, follow-on and young-child formula (regulatory_limits.csv line 33; crosswalk lines 171/178, applied to infant-formula-rtf-dairy/soy). It applies to the canned form and expressly excludes "canned dried and canned powdered products," so it does not reach the powder form HMTc-IF-PWD covers — but a formula tin ML nonetheless exists. In the section titled "How HMTc compares to law," a hostile expert or regulator can cite the EU canned-formula tin ML verbatim to rebut the sentence. The mercury half is accurate (no infant-formula mercury ML exists in any jurisdiction in the reference data), and every tin ML in the file is canned-scoped, so no tin ML applies to powdered formula. The underlying substance is unaffected — HMTc's 49/4.7 µg/kg tin limit sits ~1000x below the 50 mg/kg ML, so it is genuinely occurrence-derived — making this a precision defect rather than a substantive error, but one that should be corrected before this defensibility-critical document is published.
confirmed.fix: Qualify the tin claim to the powder form instead of asserting no jurisdiction sets any formula tin ML. Replace the sentence with: "For total mercury, no jurisdiction sets an infant-formula maximum level. For tin, no maximum level applies to powdered infant formula — the EU 2023/915 tin ML of 50 mg/kg for canned formula expressly excludes canned dried and powdered products — so the HMTc tin limit is set from measured occurrence."

confirmed.location: /private/tmp/.../scratchpad/publishable-draft.md — Section 2 limits table, Aluminium (Al) row, "Basis of the limit" column (single shared label "regulatory ceiling"); the mislabel also propagates into the Section 2 explanatory prose at lines 49–52 ("nickel, aluminium ... the applicable law sets a higher ceiling").
confirmed.problem: The Aluminium row uses one shared basis label, "regulatory ceiling," that is correct for the non-soy limit but wrong for the soy-based limit. Non-soy Al 3500 is engine-confirmed as cap-bound (standards-qc-gate-report.csv line 222: candidate 3500 = cap 3500, rationale regulatory-alignment; pooled P97 6538 was capped down). But soy-based Al 4600 is engine-confirmed as occurrence-derived, not cap-bound (line 230 and hmtc_aggregate_distributions.csv: candidate_value 4611.1205 → 4600, rationale literature-baseline, pooled_p45 4611.1205, binding below the 7000 regulatory cap). So the 4600 soy limit is a testing/occurrence baseline mislabeled as a regulatory ceiling — the reverse of the true rationale. The draft is also internally inconsistent: its printed 4600 can only come from the literature-baseline slug (the regulatory-alignment slug would print 7000), yet it labels the basis "regulatory ceiling." The lines 49–52 prose repeats the error by attributing the higher soy aluminium limit to the law's ceiling, when the 4600 value actually sits below the 7000 legal ceiling and is therefore more protective than the law — a gap the mislabel hides, contrary to the Part 2 honesty rule.
confirmed.fix: Give the Aluminium row per-subcategory basis: non-soy = "regulatory ceiling" (3500), soy-based = "testing baseline" (4600) — either by splitting the "Basis of the limit" cell/annotation for this row or by footnoting that the soy Al value is occurrence-derived and sits below the 7000 µg/kg legal ceiling. Also correct the Section 2 prose at lines 49–52 so aluminium-soy is no longer grouped with nickel as a regulatory-ceiling case (nickel-soy 400 is genuinely regulatory-alignment per gate line 231, but aluminium-soy is literature-baseline). Optionally add the soy Al row to the Section 4 "How HMTc compares to law" table (4600 vs 7000 converted) so the more-protective gap is shown.

confirmed.location: §4 "How HMTc compares to law" (draft lines 87–101) vs §3 (draft lines 76–78, "No HMTc limit exceeds the lowest maximum level in force") and the §2 soy column (draft lines 42, 44: Ni 400, Al 4600)
confirmed.problem: §3 makes an absolute claim that no HMTc limit exceeds the lowest legal maximum level in force, and §4 is the table meant to substantiate it — but §4 tabulates only the cow-milk (non-soy) column, showing Nickel ML = 250 and Aluminium = 3500. The two soy limits in §2 tagged "regulatory ceiling" (Ni 400, Al 4600) appear nowhere in §4, so a numbers-only cross-check reads soy Ni 400 as exceeding the only nickel ML shown (250) and soy Al 4600 as exceeding the only Al value shown (3500) — an apparent self-contradiction of §3, and precisely the "the standards rest on self-published numbers" attack line this document exists to foreclose. Verified against the repo: the soy values are correct, so this is a documentation gap, not a math error. EU 2024/1987 point 3.6.13.2 (wiki/regulations/eu-2024-1987-nickel-maximum-levels.md line 47) sets soy-protein-isolate formula powder Ni at 0.40 mg/kg = 400 µg/kg, so soy Ni 400 equals its own ceiling. AU/NZ Sch 19 (wiki/regulations/au-nz-food-standards-code-schedule-19-contaminants.md line 37) sets soy-based infant-formula Al at 1 mg/kg = 1000 µg/kg as-consumed, which converts on the same ×7 powder basis used for the non-soy 3500 to 7000 µg/kg, so soy Al 4600 sits below its own ceiling. The §2 prose note that "the applicable law sets a higher ceiling" for soy mitigates but does not close the gap, because §3 is stated as absolute and §4 is its proof table, which omits the soy ceilings entirely.
confirmed.fix: Add the soy legal-ceiling rows to the §4 comparison table (or split it into non-soy and soy columns) so every HMTc limit in §2 is shown at or below its own legal ceiling: Nickel — soy 400 vs EU 2024/1987 point 3.6.13.2 (0.40 mg/kg = 400 µg/kg); Aluminium — soy 4600 vs AU/NZ Food Standards Code Sch 19 soy-based infant-formula entry (1 mg/kg as-consumed = 7000 µg/kg converted to powder on the same ×7 basis as the non-soy 3500). Cite the point/entry numbers as done for the non-soy rows. Secondary check while applying: once the soy Al ceiling (7000) is shown, the §2 "regulatory ceiling" basis tag on soy Al 4600 reads oddly (4600 is well below 7000, i.e. not ceiling-bound), so confirm the soy Al value's basis and source the 7000 ceiling row from the regulation rather than inventing a number — do not relabel or move the 4600 value as part of this fix without separate verification.

confirmed.location: The phrase "derived from the cleaner part of the regulated market" is in §1 (lines 17–18) and §2 (line 47) — NOT §3 as the finding states. §3 (lines 70–74) and §6 (lines 129–131) already carry the accurate "large majority can meet" framing.
confirmed.problem: Real but minor inconsistency: §1 and §2 describe the limit as "derived from the cleaner part of the regulated market" (connoting a select subset), while §6 says ~four in five (80%) brands already meet it. Under the program's P97 clean-subcategory methodology the limit sits near the top of the distribution where most products already pass, so "cleaner part" mildly misdescribes it. However, the finding is substantially wrong on mechanism and severity: it attributes the offending phrase to §3, but §3 contains no such language — §3 explicitly says the clean subcategory limit is one "a large majority of well-controlled brands can meet," which AGREES with §6 rather than undercutting it. §6 also already defends the ratchet head-on ("initial standard," "designed to fall," "that trajectory"), pre-empting the "low bar" attack. So this is a lead-section wording polish, not the major contradiction claimed, and the accurate framing already exists in the document.
confirmed.fix: Align §1/§2 to the accurate framing already in §3/§6: replace "the cleaner part of the regulated market" with wording that the limit is a level a large majority of well-controlled brands can already meet by design — the ratchet's deliberate starting point — with ongoing selectivity coming from the scheduled tightening, not the initial pass rate. Do NOT touch §3 or §6; §3 is already correct and §6's trajectory language is the strongest part of the ratchet story. Ignore the finding's claim that §3 needs changing.
